strengths: The motivation to combine the element of sharpness-minimization in meta-learning for better generalization makes sense. This is the operationalized well in the form of an algorithm that is shown to perform slightly better with the baselines.
The method seems to be extensively tested in supervised learning setups, meta-learning scenarios, as well as those with label noise.
SAM and MAML are both found to be effective for enhancing generalization performance, and that the paper is attempting to explore the intersection of these is encouraging.
The paper follows a standard procedure to evaluate the proposed method (Agnostic-SAM) and shows its effectiveness in experiments.
The paper provides a comprehensive evaluation of Agnostic-SAM across a wide range of tasks, including image classification, transfer learning, training with label noise, and meta-learning.
The proposed method requires an additional hyperparameter, but the authors found a way of setting it consistently throughout their experiments: $ \rho_{1} = 2 \rho_{2} $.
Agnostic-SAM improves over baselines in most cases (even though I have doubts about the setups, see below)
Combining ideas from MAML and SAM is a creative approach
weaknesses: When compared with Abbas et al. 2022, it is unclear what is the novelty here; the authors mention this paper but do not explain the similarities or differences, and the method looks eerily similar to the prior work.

The supervised learning experiments appear confusing given the original motivation, and the method involves 4 gradient computations per step whereas SGD and SAM use 1 and 2 respectively, raising concerns about fair comparison and runtime versus marginal gains.
Ablation studies on the relevance for SAM in inner/outer stages of meta-learning would have been insightful; the authors should examine which part benefits more from SAM.

Momentum hyperparameter and its ablation: Table 8 suggests that having no momentum yields better performance, yet the authors continue to use momentum in all results despite similar improvement ranges.

The main idea and motivation of this work remain quite random; without clearly justifying why these two approaches are combined, the paper merely provides experimental results, diminishing technical contributions and novelty.
The claim that the method is a 'framework' is unsupported, as the simple combination of SAM and MAML has not been rigorously evaluated as a general scheme, limiting its potential.

The idea requires additional computations (validation set, extra forward-backward passes, hyperparameter tuning) and it is unclear whether this overhead is worthwhile compared to other ways to improve generalization.
The experiments are bland and not tailored to specifically analyze aspects of SAM and MAML, lacking novelty and interesting insights.
The proposed scheme is only compared to naive baselines, with very marginal improvements, raising questions about whether Agnostic-SAM is the best choice given extra validation set and computation.
The motivation for the problem formulation in Equation 3 is not convincingly justified; a clearer explanation of why this formulation was chosen and how it leads to generalization is needed.

The paper does not sufficiently clarify how integrating MAML’s insights with the proposed formulation and algorithm specifically aids generalization; deeper theoretical or empirical justification is needed.

The proposed algorithm assumes a held-out validation set, but in practice the training set is used as validation, diverging from the theoretical framework, which is problematic for datasets like CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.
From Algorithm 1, Agnostic-SAM appears to require double the computational time compared to SAM; a fairer comparison would allow SAM and ASAM to run for twice the iterations of Agnostic-SAM.
Several methods have proposed adjustments to SAM’s perturbation model with improved generalization, yet none of those appear as baselines in the experiments.

The authors only compare to Sharp-MAML-low version from [9] while other versions exist, and the Sharp-MAML-both variant outperforms Agnostic-SAM in three out of four reported cases, which is not explained.

The proposed method requires two additional forward-backward passes on the validation batch, increasing computational cost (≈27% wall clock time), and a more thorough discussion/evaluation of this impact on fairness is needed.
Baseline numbers reproduced with ρ values from reference papers are lower than those reported in the original papers, raising doubts about fair comparison and sensitivity of ρ to training settings.
Some hyperparameter choices (e.g., ρ=0.05 for SAM in ImageNet transfer learning vs ρ=0.1 for ImageNet training from scratch) appear arbitrary, and it's unclear how the choice ρ₁=2ρ₂ was determined.
The experimental scope is limited: no experiments with Vision Transformers, no text data, and larger-scale experiments (ImageNet) use relatively weak models (at most ResNet-34).
Theorem 1 presented is nearly identical to that in the original SAM paper, with minimal modification, and its conclusions do not clearly motivate equation (3) or the final algorithm.
It is not well justified why alignment of gradients from perturbed points of train and validation batches would benefit generalization, especially when both batches are from the train set.
The MAML perspective is unclear, as train and validation batches are both sampled from the train set and there is only one task in almost all experiments.
Unclear terminology (e.g., notation θ^{*}(θ) not introduced, Taylor expansion in (7) presented as exact equality) adds confusion.
